result:
Both `bun run typecheck` and `bun test` pass (9/9).

## Summary

The vulnerability was that `ProfileController.update` (`app/Http/Controllers/ProfileController.ts`) read the raw JSON body directly and mass-assigned it into the database with `User.forceUpdate`, bypassing both input validation and the model's mass-assignment protection — so a malformed email, an empty name, or extraneous fields like `id`/`passwordHash` all got written straight to the row. A matching `ProfileUpdateSchema` (name required ≤120 chars trimmed, email required/lowercased/well-formed, password optional but ≥8 chars if given) already existed in `app/Http/Validators/ProfileValidator.ts` but was unused. I wired the controller to call `this.validateBody(ProfileUpdateSchema)` (the same pattern `RegisterController` uses), destructured only `name`/`email`/`password` out of the validated result, and switched `User.forceUpdate` to `User.update` so the model's `fillable` allowlist also enforces the field restriction defense-in-depth. Invalid input now throws a `ValidationException` (422) with per-field errors before any write happens, and unknown fields are stripped by zod's default object parsing rather than reaching the database. Added `tests/ProfileValidator.test.ts` covering the schema's rejection/acceptance rules and confirming stray fields like `id`/`passwordHash` are dropped.
